column3: Exact concluding reliance formula; within the same setting, threatened failure is met by divine guardianship rather than self-sufficiency.
The pledged victory of the supported host directly extends the aid-to-prevailing relation, with the channel also framing a gathered support force.
Places prophetic opposition alongside sufficient guidance and help, showing enemies need not negate effective divine support; the auxiliary human-helper reading remains secondary.
Exactly repeats reliance on God, but adds little beyond the prior card about help being granted or withdrawn.
The immediately preceding context joins consultation, resolve, and reliance, so trust follows collective deliberation and action rather than replacing them.
Defeat is a temporary condition, usefully qualifying any fixed reading of prevailing, though it does not identify the source of reversal.
Makes aid reciprocal: committed human action is answered by divine support that steadies movement, without collapsing either side into the other.
The hostile side's spending ends in loss and defeat; the branch reading gives a contrary case in which apparent resources do not secure effective support.
Its question exposes a network that produces no mutual aid, a negative parallel to the focus ayah's question about any helper after abandonment.
Challenges the claim that a gathered army can independently help; the secondary reading keeps alternative helpers as dependent rather than simply absent.
The favor to Moses and Aaron enters the rescue-and-victory branch, but this opening statement alone supplies less of the focus relation than later cards.
The lexical overlap concerns dense gardens; the mixed auxiliary resonance is too remote to materially clarify help, abandonment, or reliance.
Messengers deny independent authority and direct believers to rely on God, adding authorization by permission to the focus's reliance command.
A self-described united force claims mutual victory; this is a useful rival model of collective strength, but the evidence is explicitly mixed.
A written declaration that God and the messengers prevail grounds victory in divine resolve; the additional image of coordinated force remains a secondary parallel.
What God opens cannot be withheld and what He withholds cannot be sent after Him; this is a close structural parallel to aid and abandonment.
Organized obstruction seeks to win by preventing reception of recitation, a contrary strategy that shows victory can be pursued through disrupted communication rather than real support.
Announces defeat for opponents, but the auxiliary reading is mixed and the verse adds less to the aid-and-reliance mechanism than earlier cards.
Recalls a hostile reach being restrained and immediately commands reliance, concretely linking protection from threat with trust in God.
The supported messengers are declared victorious, reinforcing the pledged pattern but substantially repeating the earlier adjacent card.
A defeated servant asks the Lord for aid without prescribing its means, preserving divine agency while leaving the mode of help open.
Denies that any protector or helper can independently shield against God's harm or mercy, directly sharpening the focus ayah's exclusive-source claim.
Divine help results in prevailing within the rescue branch, but it repeats the same cluster already established by the preceding cards.
Human hands enact the conflict while God is said to help, preserving mediated human action rather than treating it as an independent source.
Harmful whispering has no effect except by God's permission, and the verse returns to reliance; it extends trust to hidden social harm rather than battlefield defeat.
The cry of one described as overcome asks for divine intervention, directly pairing human incapacity with an appeal beyond the apparent balance of force.
Loyalty is made conditional on visible victory; the auxiliary reversal makes this a useful contrast, though its full reversal lies beyond this ayah itself.
A promise that none can overcome the group is exposed as deceptive when the alleged protector withdraws, a direct contrary image to reliable divine help.
The prior word to the messengers introduces the promise sequence, but its content is supplied by the following cards rather than this ayah alone.
God's ownership and power over life and death leave no protector or helper besides Him, extending the focus's exclusivity beyond a conflict scene.
A small force can prevail over a larger one by God's permission, directly countering numerical strength as the decisive explanation; endurance remains part of the scene.
Regret over intimate attachment enters the isolation branch, but only indirectly bears on the focus ayah's support and abandonment relation.
The competitors seek reward for prevailing; the auxiliary reading preserves the later reversal, but this largely duplicates the prior victory-conditioned allegiance card.
The shared interrogative wording concerns a good loan, not help, abandonment, prevailing, or reliance.
The summons scene belongs to a relevant channel branch but does not itself clarify the focus ayah's causal account of aid.
Alignment with God, the messenger, and believers is associated with prevailing, offering a collective-side parallel while the evidence remains mixed.
The verbal overlap is the good-loan formula and contributes no direct evidence about the focus relation.
Rescue from severe distress supplies a concrete outcome in the favor branch, though it is less explicit about help and prevailing than its neighboring cards.
Mutual patrons cannot help one another at the decisive time; the auxiliary reading preserves the contrast with the sole effective mercy rather than treating all aid alike.
God is prevailing over His affair despite local plans, adding an overarching governance dimension but not the focus ayah's direct appeal to reliance.
The abandoner leaves a person after leading them astray; within its channel's isolation reading, it is a direct negative parallel to divine abandonment.
Those cut off by God's curse find no helper, supporting the consequence side of abandonment, though the causal setting differs from the focus ayah.
No one could sustain the heavens and earth after God; this cosmic non-replaceability closely parallels the question of a helper after divine withdrawal.
The difficult-day response is in the relevant summons branch, but it adds no distinct account of help, defeat, or reliance.
A claim to prevail turns into defeat and humiliation in the same arena, a compact reversal of apparent strength.
Hostility within family relations may complicate reliance, but this ayah gives no explicit support or abandonment relation.
The messenger's complaint of abandonment belongs to the isolation branch, yet its object is the Quran rather than the focus ayah's aid relation.
Explicitly locates help with God while retaining an outward means that reassures hearts; the auxiliary reading preserves that means as channel, not source.
Its lexical overlap does not bear on aid, abandonment, prevailing, or reliance.
Employment and allegiance are conditioned on victory; it repeats the competitive pattern, with the auxiliary reversal remaining relevant but secondary.
The shared reference to later discourse does not supply a support, abandonment, prevailing, or reliance relation.
Commanded entry precedes confidence of prevailing and is joined to reliance on God, closely combining action, risk, and trust.
The overlap is limited to general God-language and voluntary action, without a support-related connection.
The same reward is attached to being killed or prevailing, making outcome less determinative; this is a useful secondary qualification of victory.
Despite general divine language, the legal and communal-completion content does not materially explain aid, abandonment, or reliance.
No protector or helper exists apart from God, a close exclusivity parallel, though it largely repeats the point already made in 9:116 and 33:17.
Wealth and children do not furnish a meaningful connection to the focus ayah.
An oath of victory seeks to declare the result in advance; it reinforces the contrast between asserted dominance and the source of actual outcome.
The occurrence of believer language is not enough to connect this legal ruling to the focus relation.
No protector or helper exists besides God in earth or heaven, repeating the exclusive-source pattern in a broader setting.
Divine provision addresses fear of loss, but this is only an indirect parallel to reliance after help or abandonment.
The lack of helpers for wrongdoers is present, while the verse's main concern is accountable giving and vows rather than the focus relation.
Faithful work and its recording do not offer a substantive aid, abandonment, or prevailing link.
Completes the prior defeat-to-victory sequence, preserving reversal over time but still leaving the source of prevailing unstated here.
Individual burden-bearing and self-purification are not materially connected to the focus ayah.
Putative helpers can neither help their followers nor defend themselves, directly rejecting both external support and self-rescue as alternatives.
The shared language of later discourse does not yield a relevant support connection.
Those led astray have no helpers; the auxiliary reading adds directional failure, but the relation to the focus ayah remains indirect.
Associating another god ends in being abandoned and blamed, providing a direct abandonment consequence while not specifying help in conflict.
No one is helped in the judgment scene; its individual-responsibility reading is relevant only as a distant limit on transferable support.
The lineage or party relation in this ayah does not clarify help, abandonment, prevailing, or reliance.
A promised support network repeatedly fails in pledge, action, and aftermath, offering a detailed contrary model of ineffective human backing.
Even a numerous faction cannot avail its members, while God is with believers; this directly separates headcount from effective support.
God's sovereignty is paired with the absence of any protector or helper besides Him, though it repeats the earlier exclusivity formulation.
God's sufficiency is expressed through divine aid and believers together, preserving a layered support arrangement rather than an either-or source model.
The question who could help the messenger against God makes treatment of vulnerable believers answerable to divine authority; it is a moral application of help's limit.
Immediately adjacent to the focus context, divine help at Badr while the believers were weak makes victory non-self-generated and connects it to grateful God-consciousness.
Severe trial can coexist with the nearness of God's help, qualifying any reading that divine support excludes hardship or delay.
Divine decree and guardianship culminate in the same reliance formula; despite formulaic redundancy, it expands trust to all that befalls the believers.
The concise promise of mighty help confirms divine support but adds little mechanism after the stronger earlier formulations.
The prayer instruction does not materially develop the focus ayah's relation.
The repeated judgment-day denial of aid adds no new material beyond 2:48 and remains distant from the focus context.
Opportunistic claims to share a God-given opening show unstable alliance behavior, but the focus relation is only indirect.
A facing force asks for patience, steadiness, and victory from God, closely joining inner endurance and divine help in active conflict.
Communal repair and obedience may frame believers' conduct, but this ayah has no explicit aid or prevailing relation.
The alleged objects of reliance can help neither their adherents nor themselves, a direct parallel to the focus's challenge about a helper after divine abandonment.
Reliance is maintained after guidance and amid injury, with patience explicitly retained; this extends trust into sustained opposition rather than mere outcome.
God as patron and excellent helper directly supports the focus claim, but its compressed formulation largely repeats the established exclusive-source pattern.
The command for entrusted authority and just judgment has no material aid or reliance connection.
Unsupported worship produces no helper for wrongdoers; this directly negates rival support, while the critique of baseless worship supplies its specific setting.
God can permit hostile power yet peace removes a route of action; this is an indirect limit on conflict, not a clear aid or abandonment reading.
People are tested by whether they support God and messengers without seeing, linking commitment to justice and force while preserving the distinct direction of their support.
The warning against fabricating lies does not materially address help, abandonment, prevailing, or reliance.
At the decisive time, cries cannot obtain help; this gives a temporal limit to aid, though it is far from the believers' reliance setting.
The historical report of rejecting messengers does not by itself add a support-related reading.
Mutual protection arises through migration, shelter, and aid, yet the treaty limit remains operative; both cooperative and bounded readings are retained.
Remembering through fear offers no substantive link to the focus ayah.
The closing prayer combines capacity, pardon, mercy, guardianship, and a request for victory, integrating reliance with sustained human responsibility.
The command to fear God and obey does not materially clarify the aid-and-abandonment relation.
Those expected to help cannot do so and their worshippers become their attendant forces, reversing the assumed direction of support.
Directs believers to seek help through patience and prayer, adding disciplined means of reliance rather than a claim of autonomous strength.
Names God as the protector of believers, supplying the guardianship frame that underlies the focus ayah's reliance command.
Identifies God as protector of believers, a concise but direct parallel to the exclusive patronage assumed in 3:160.
In the immediate battle context, promised reinforcement addresses believers' weakness and makes divine support concrete without making them its source.
Patience and God-consciousness are joined to further reinforcement, preserving both human endurance and divine aid as distinct factors.
Explicitly says the reinforcement is reassurance and that victory is only from God, making it one of the clearest interpretive parallels.
Forbids weakness and grief while describing believers as higher; it qualifies prevailing as a faith-conditioned stance, though it lacks the aid formula.
Prophetic companions do not weaken or yield under adversity, adding durable human steadfastness as a parallel condition around divine support.
A battle prayer asks for forgiveness, firm feet, and help, directly joining moral repair, steadiness, and requested victory.
States that God is the believers' protector and the best of helpers, an exact near-context answer to the focus ayah's question about any helper after Him.
The battle narrative explicitly links fulfillment of God's promise with subsequent faltering and dispute, directly illuminating the focus context's support and withdrawal language.
Answers intimidation with God's sufficiency and reliance on Him, a central missing counterpart to 3:160's final command.
Rejects fear of the threatening ally and redirects fear to God, adding a contrary pressure on the reliance demanded in the focus ayah.
God's knowledge of enemies is paired with His sufficiency as protector and helper, closely echoing the focus ayah's exclusive-source logic.
Believers seek aid from their Lord and receive an answer, directly depicting the appeal-and-response side of divine help.
Recalls believers as few and vulnerable before God sheltered, strengthened, and provided for them, a concrete reversal of exposure into support.
Commands steadfastness and remembrance when meeting a force, supplying a practical believer-side discipline alongside the focus ayah's reliance.
Links obedience, unity, patience, and avoidance of failure, showing how internal dispute can dissipate effective collective force.
A large number does not avail the believers at Hunayn, directly warning against numerical strength as a sufficient explanation of victory.
Divine tranquility and unseen forces follow the failure of numerical confidence, supplying a concrete help-and-reversal sequence.
Even if people do not support the messenger, God has supported him, directly distinguishing divine help from unreliable human backing.
Believing men and women are mutual protectors, adding a social form of solidarity that remains distinct from ultimate divine aid.
God is with the God-conscious and excellent-doers, offering a concise presence relation that can accompany but does not replace the focus ayah's aid formula.
A destroyed possessor has no group to help him against God and cannot defend himself, strongly paralleling the impossibility of a helper after divine withdrawal.
Locates patronage with God alone and describes Him as best in reward and outcome, reinforcing the exclusive-protector reading.
Challenges who can guard people from the Merciful by night or day, a protective parallel to the focus ayah's rhetorical question.
Describes a supposed patron and helper as evil, preserving a contrary reading in which claimed support is itself ruinous.
Directly takes up the question of whether God will help His servant, making divine support a contested but explicit subject.
States that God defends believers, a close protection parallel even though its wording is not the focus ayah's help-and-abandonment formula.
Promises that God will surely help those who help Him and affirms divine strength, strongly extending the reciprocal-aid pattern of 47:7.
When a powerful figure falls, neither his faction nor he can secure help, furnishing a clear contrary example of failed worldly backing.
Commands believers to remember divine favor when forces attacked and God sent wind and unseen forces, a direct battle-support episode.
The sight of the confederates increases believers in faith and submission, adding an internal response to threat rather than an autonomous victory claim.
God turns back the hostile force without believers needing to fight, sharply separating decisive outcome from apparent human force.
Asks who could help against God's punishment if it comes, directly restating the limit on all alternative support.
Promises help for messengers and believers in worldly life and at testimony, a broad direct statement of divine support.
Whoever God leaves astray has no protector after Him, an abandonment parallel that should remain distinct from the focus ayah's battlefield setting.
Denies protectors who can help apart from God, repeating the exclusive-source claim in a judgmental setting.
Challenges why supposed gods did not help their adherents, a direct negative parallel to reliance on any helper besides God.
God is protector of believers while disbelievers have no protector, adding a direct patronage contrast.
Combines a call not to weaken with God's presence, extending the believer-side perseverance dimension of prevailing.
God sends tranquility into believers' hearts and possesses the forces of the heavens and earth, connecting inner strengthening with divine resources.
God's forces belong to Him and His might is affirmed, giving a source-of-force frame while remaining less explicit about aid than nearby verses.
Opponents who fight are said to turn away and find neither protector nor helper, a strong contrary case to the focus ayah's rhetorical question.
Believers are called to be helpers of God; one group is then supported and prevails, extending reciprocal support into collective identity.
Whoever relies on God finds Him sufficient, an exceptionally direct missing counterpart to the focus ayah's command to rely on God.
The messenger denies any protector or refuge apart from God, reinforcing the nonreplaceability of divine protection in a different setting.
